input.question: If the sensation of pain is there to tell us we have been damaged, why are serious injuries usually accompanied by such crippling pain that we are unable to move/do anything about the injury?
input.ground_truth: The pain is usually there to keep you from moving and making things worse. In an actual emergency the body releasing pain-blocking chemicals that will allow you to ignore the pain so you can do what you need to in order to survive.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If the sensation of pain is there to tell us we have been damaged, why are serious injuries usually accompanied by such crippling pain that we are unable to move/do anything about the injury?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine your body is like a house, and you are the person who lives there. Now, if something breaks in your house, like a window, you want to know about it right away, so you don’t get hurt more, right? So, your body has special “alarm bells” called nerves. When you get hurt—like if you fall and scrape your knee—those alarm bells ring really, really loud to tell you, “Hey! Something is wrong here!”

But if the scrape is very big or the injury is serious, your body gets extra worried. It makes the alarm bells ring super loud and maybe even makes your leg feel so ouchie that you can’t move it. That’s because your body is trying super hard to protect you from getting hurt even more. It’s like when you get a really bad boo-boo and your mom says, “Don’t move! Let me help you!” Your body is being like your mom, telling you to stop and not do anything until it’s safe.

So, the pain is there to warn you and protect you, but when it’s really bad, it makes you stop moving so you don’t make the injury worse.
